content: The Shape of the Thing - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Shape of the Thing Where we are right now, and what likely happens next Ethan Mollick Mar 12, 2026 839 63 74 Share In October of 2023, I wrote about the “Shape of the Shadow of the Thing,” speculating on the Thing that AI might turn into in the coming years. I think we can see the Thing much more clearly now, and some of the consequences that come with it. As I have been discussing in recent posts, we have entered a new phase of AI. After ChatGPT was introduced, human-AI work took the form of what I called co-intelligence, where humans would prompt AI back-and-forth to get help on tasks. Starting in late 2025, we entered a new era thanks to AI agents like Claude Code , OpenAI’s Codex, and OpenClaw. These are AI systems that you can just give work to, sometimes hours of human work, and get back reasonable and useful results in minutes. This is an era of managing AIs, rather than working with them. This new approach to AI is the outcome of the rapid exponential improvement in AI abilities. That means you can’t understand where we are, and where we might be going, without understanding the increasing capability of AI. Riding up the Exponential Exponential improvements are hard to visualize, so rather than charts or graphs, I want to start with otters. If you have followed my writing on AI, you know about my Otter Test , where I challenge various AI image models to show a picture of an “otter on a plane using wifi.” As you can see below, the progress from 2022 (the year ChatGPT launched) to 2025 was rapid and remarkable. So, what has happened in the time since that April, 2025 image? With nearly perfect images, video has become the new frontier and has also seen exponential gains. To demonstrate, I gave the most advanced (and still unreleased in the US) AI video model from TikTok maker Bytedance, the prompt: A documentary about how otters view Ethan Mollick's "Otter Test" which judges AIs by their ability to create images of otters sitting in planes . This is the very first result — definitely turn on your sound: Aside from a single pronunciation mistake, this is pretty perfect, down to the fact that the otters are animated to have human-like expressions. Of course, video models are cool, but they are not necessarily indicative of what useful agentic AI can do. So, what if we look at the benchmarks of AI ability, do we see the same exponential curve? We certainly do in the most famous evaluation in AI today, the METR Long Tasks graph . It tries to measure AI progress by seeing how much human work an AI can complete autonomously with some measure of reliability. It has attracted its share of critics, and even METR has pointed out potential issues . But if you don’t like the METR graph, you will find most graphs of AI ability have that same curve. content: A Guide to Which AI to Use in the Agentic Era One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in A Guide to Which AI to Use in the Agentic Era It's not just chatbots anymore Ethan Mollick Feb 18, 2026 1,769 122 190 Share I have written eight of these guides since ChatGPT came out, but this version represents a very large break with the past, because what it means to “use AI” has changed dramatically. Until a few months ago, for the vast majority of people, “using AI” meant talking to a chatbot in a back-and-forth conversation. But over the past few months, it has become practical to use AI as an agent: you can assign them to a task and they do them, using tools as appropriate. Because of this change, you have to consider three things when deciding what AI to use: Models, Apps, and Harnesses. The exact same model, Claude Opus 4.6, asked the exact same question, “Compare ChatGPT and Claude and Gemini” in three different apps and harnesses. With no harness the information is out of date, on the Claude.ai site I get updated information and verifiable sources, using Claude Cowork, I get a sophisticated analysis and well-formatted head-to-head comparisons Models are the underlying AI brains, and the big three are GPT-5.2/5.3, Claude Opus 4.6, and Gemini 3 Pro (the companies are releasing new models much more rapidly than the past, so version numbers may change in the coming weeks). These are what determine how smart the system is, how well it reasons, how good it is at writing or coding or analyzing a spreadsheet, and how well it can see images or create them. Models are what the benchmarks measure and what the AI companies race to improve. When people say “Claude is better at writing” or “ChatGPT is better at math,” they’re talking about models. Apps are the products you actually use to talk to a model, and which let models do real work for you. The most common app is the website for each of these models: chatgpt.com, claude.ai, gemini.google.com (or else their equivalent application on your phone). Increasingly, there are other apps made by each of these AI companies as well, including coding tools like OpenAI Codex or Claude Code, and desktop tools like Claude Cowork. Harnesses are what let the power of AI models do real work, like a horse harness takes the raw power of the horse and lets it pull a cart or plow. A harness is a system that lets the AI use tools, take actions, and complete multi-step tasks on its own. Apps come with a harness. Claude on the website has a harness that lets Claude 4.6 Opus do web searches and write code but also has instructions about how to approach various problems like creating spreadsheets or doing graphic design work. Claude Code has an even more extensive harness: it gives Claude 4.6 Opus a virtual computer, a web browser, a code terminal, and the ability to string these together to actually do stuff like researching, building, and testing your new website from scratch. content: Management as AI superpower - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in Management as AI superpower Thriving in a world of agentic AI Ethan Mollick Jan 27, 2026 987 99 97 Share I just taught an experimental class at the University of Pennsylvania where I challenged students to create a startup from scratch in four days. Most of the people in the class were in the executive MBA program, so they were taking classes while also working as doctors, managers, or leaders in a variety of large and small companies. Few had ever coded. I introduced them to Claude Code and Google Antigravity, which they needed to use to build a working prototype. But a prototype alone is not a startup, so they used ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to accelerate the idea generation, market research, competitive positioning, pitching, and financial modelling processes. I was curious how far they could get in such a short time. It turns out they got very far. Examples of demos: Ticket Passport (a market for verified ticket sales) by Dee Sethmajhi , Jane Lian Wang , and Yue Ma . Revenue Resilience (Identifies at-risk revenue for small businesses and creates agentic solutions) by Whit Chiles , Jose Olivares , and S pencer Louie . Parenting companion (matching kid interests to activities) by Manoj Massand , Samuel Lee , and Harry Lu. Invive (blood sugar prediction) by Angela Argentati , Sabeen Chawla , and Adeel Rizwan . (There were lots of other great ones, but these teams gave me permission to share screenshots!) I’ve been teaching entrepreneurship for a decade and a half, and I've seen thousands of startup ideas (some of which turned into large companies) so I have a good sense of the expectations for what a class of smart MBA students can accomplish. I would estimate that what I saw in a couple of days was an order of magnitude further along the path to a real startup than I had seen out of students working over a full semester before AI. Most of the prototypes were not just sample screens but actually had a core feature working. Ideas were far more diverse and interesting than usual. Market and customer analyses were insightful. It was really impressive. These were not yet working startups nor were they fully operational products (with a couple exceptions) — but they had shaved months and huge amounts of money and effort from the traditional process. And there was something else: most early startups need to pivot, changing direction as they learn more about what the market wants and what is technically possible. By lowering the costs of pivoting, it was much easier to explore the possibilities without being locked in or even explore multiple startups at once: you just tell the AI what you want. I wish I could say this impressive output was the result of my brilliant teaching, but we don’t really have a great framework yet for how to use all these tools, the students largely figured it out on their own. content: AI to ROI Reports & Data: Boston Consulting Group Reports CEOs are Taking the Lead in AI AI to ROI - By Ray Rike and Peter Buchanan Subscribe Sign in AI to ROI Reports & Data: Boston Consulting Group Reports CEOs are Taking the Lead in AI Boston Consulting Group Report: The Business Impact of CEOs Who Champion AI Ray Rike and Peter Buchanan Mar 19, 2026 1 Share AI Spending Is Soaring and CEOs Are Taking Charge per Boston Consulting Group Report About the Authors The report is a joint publication of Boston Consulting Group (BCG) and BCG X, the firm’s technology build and design unit. BCG is one of the world’s leading management consulting firms, founded in 1963 and active in more than 50 countries. The report was co-authored by Christoph Schweizer , CEO of BCG and a member of the firm’s Executive and Operating Committees, where he has led the firm’s global growth strategy since 2021. His co-author, Sylvain Duranton , is Global Leader of BCG X and a Senior Partner with three decades of experience leading AI and analytics implementations for major organizations worldwide. Purpose and Methodology AI Radar 2026 is the third annual edition of BCG’s flagship study on the global state of artificial intelligence in business. Its purpose is to: Track how corporate AI investment, leadership, and strategy are evolving year over year. To identify the behavior’s that separate high-performing organizations from the rest. The report is based on a survey of 2,360 executives conducted across 16 markets and nine industries, including 640 CEOs . Respondents represent companies with annual revenues ranging from $100 million to over $5 billion . Markets surveyed include the US, UK, France, Germany, Japan, India, China, and several Middle East and African countries. The survey was fielded in late 2025 and published in January 2026. Key Takeaways The report identifies three central findings that describe a decisive shift in how companies are approaching AI in 2026. Corporate AI investment has doubled year over year and shows no sign of slowing, even among companies that have yet to see a return. Ownership of AI strategy has moved firmly from the CIO to the CEO, with chief executives now personally driving transformation agendas. A clear taxonomy of CEO behavior has emerged, with a small group of high-conviction leaders, identified as Trailblazers, pulling meaningfully ahead of their peers. A Deeper Dive AI Investment Has Doubled and Is Here to Stay Companies plan to spend approximately 1.7% of annual revenues on AI in 2026 , which is more than double the 0.8% reported in 2025. This surge draws from budgets well beyond the traditional IT envelope . Technology firms lead with 2.1% of revenue , followed by financial institutions at 2.0% and insurance at 1.9%. Every sector surveyed increased its planned allocation. 94% of organizations say they will continue spending at current or higher levels even if 2026 initiatives fail to deliver a financial return. content: AI to ROI Metric: Accuracy and Quality Improvement AI to ROI - By Ray Rike and Peter Buchanan Subscribe Sign in AI to ROI Metric: Accuracy and Quality Improvement Measure the improvement in correctness, precision, and output quality Ray Rike and Peter Buchanan Mar 18, 2026 2 Share Accuracy and Quality Improvement Definition Accuracy measures the improvement in correctness, precision, and output quality when using AI compared to traditional methods, typically expressed as a reduction in error rate or an increase in quality score. How It Is Used Quality leaders track accuracy improvements to reduce rework costs, improve customer satisfaction, minimize error-related risk, and validate that AI systems meet or exceed human performance standards. Calculation Formula Accuracy Improvement = (AI Accuracy Rate - Baseline Accuracy Rate) / (100% - Baseline Accuracy Rate) × 100 Baseline Accuracy: Historical error rates or quality scores from manual processes AI Accuracy Rate: Error rates or quality scores with AI implementation Defect Reduction: Decrease in errors, mistakes, or quality failures Rework Costs Avoided: Labor and materials saved by reducing errors False Positive/Negative Rates: Balance between missed issues and false alarms Why This Metric Matters Accuracy improvements prevent costly errors, rework, and customer dissatisfaction. In manufacturing, reducing defect rates from 2.5% to 0.4% on $50M in annual production saves $1.05M in scrap and rework costs. Beyond direct savings, higher accuracy improves customer trust, reduces liability risk, and enables premium positioning. In critical applications such as medical diagnosis or financial fraud, improvements in accuracy directly prevent harm and financial loss. Executive Usage by Role Chief Quality Officer: Primary owner of quality and accuracy metrics across operations COO: Evaluates the accuracy impact on operational efficiency and customer satisfaction Chief Risk Officer: Assesses how accuracy improvements reduce error-related risks and liability CEO: Uses accuracy as an indicator of operational excellence and competitive differentiation Customers: Experience improved product quality and service reliability Performance Benchmarks Poor Performance: Below 20% error reduction - Marginal quality improvement Average Performance: 20-40% error reduction - Meaningful quality gains Good Performance: 40-65% error reduction - Significant quality improvement Great Performance: Above 65% error reduction - Exceptional quality approaching perfection Note: Accuracy targets depend on baseline performance and application criticality. Moving from 90% to 95% accuracy (5% error reduction) matters more in high-stakes decisions than in low-consequence tasks. Always balance accuracy with false-positive rates. The pick from last week’s Around the Horn issue is: CAICT launches its first batch of AI Safety/Security Assessments of 2026 . Based on the announcement, Chinese companies are now invited to register to have their models assessed. The evaluations take place in June and July, and then they will issue certificates and publicize results.
